title: The nuns return
hook: since the late twentieth century, full ordination for women has been renewed in several lineages; views on it differ
carry: taking the old story at its word

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ambedkar's vows, a Buddhism built on equality for everyone. Your line: equal.

Shaved heads, robes the color of turmeric, a line of women walking slowly into an ordination hall while monks wait inside to receive them. Scenes like this have happened in Sri Lanka, in Thailand, in the West, and each one has made news inside the Buddhist world. Why? Women have shaved their heads and kept precepts in Buddhist countries for a long time. But a fully ordained nun, a bhikkhuni, is something else. In some lineages that order had disappeared, and nobody alive could pass it on.
screen: `WOMEN WALK INTO THE HALL.` → `WHY IS THIS NEWS?` → `A LINE THAT HAD BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old story. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, Mahapajapati, the woman who raised the Buddha, asks him to let women go forth. He hesitates. She and other women cut their hair, put on robes and follow him anyway, on foot, until their feet are swollen and dusty. Ananda speaks for them and asks whether women can reach awakening. The Buddha says they can. So the order of nuns begins, with extra rules that place the nuns under the monks. Here's the difficulty. Full ordination is handed on by people who already have it, monks and nuns together. In the Theravada lands, the nuns' order died out or never took firm root, and in Tibet it seems never to have been brought in at all. Women kept practicing, as eight-precept or ten-precept nuns, without full ordination. Then, in our own time, women from Sri Lanka, Thailand and elsewhere received full ordination, sometimes with help from Chinese and Korean nuns, whose line had continued. Views differ, and the people who hold them are sincere. Some Theravada monks and scholars say a broken line can't be restored from outside, so these ordinations don't count under the rules. Others say the Buddha himself opened the door to women, and the rules allow it to be opened again. Tibetan teachers have studied the question at length. Some nuns are glad to keep their present vows and want no change. It's a real argument about keeping faith with rules handed down from teacher to student. And whatever any monastery decides, the women walking into those halls are taking the old story at its word.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `ORDINATION PASSES PERSON TO PERSON.` · `THE NUNS' LINE BREAKS, THEN RETURNS.` · `SINCERE VIEWS ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `WOMEN CAN AWAKEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind Mahapajapati on that long road, her feet sore, still walking, or any woman who gave her life to practice when it wasn't easy; you don't need her name. Let a little respect rise for her, the way you'd stand when someone walks into a room. When the mind wanders, come back to her steps.
Bhikkhuni. The full ordination for women, lost in some lineages and renewed in some, while sincere teachers still differ about it.
Your line: taking the old story at its word. The Buddha said women can awaken, and they keep walking in. Day one thousand seventeen, done.

howItsDone: In some Theravada and Mahayana communities women now receive full bhikkhuni ordination from monks and nuns together; in others women live as eight- or ten-precept nuns, and the question of renewal is discussed openly and settled differently by different communities.

chat.says: Why is it news when Buddhist women get ordained? Haven't there always been nuns?
options: Women kept precepts, but full ordination passes person to person, and in some lineages it broke.
Women weren't allowed to practice in any Buddhist country until very recently.
The Buddha refused women outright, so every nun today is a modern invention.
chat.meaning: Women practiced as eight- or ten-precept nuns, but full ordination is handed on by those who have it, and in some lineages that line had broken.

Mahapajapati.meaning: the woman who raised the Buddha; she asked to go forth

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's attendant, who spoke up for the women

Theravada.meaning: the way of the elders, the school of Sri Lanka and Thailand

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga X (the going forth of Mahapajapati)

notes: Mahapajapati story paraphrased from Cullavagga X / AN 8.51: shaved heads, robes, swollen feet, Ananda's question, the Buddha's answer that women can attain the fruits. Confirm details and that 'extra rules placing nuns under monks' fairly summarizes the garudhammas.

Claim that the Theravada bhikkhuni order died out and that full ordination for women was never established in Tibet: confirm wording ('seems never to have been brought in'). No dates given on purpose.
Renewed ordinations (Sri Lanka, Thailand, the West) with help from Chinese/Korean (Dharmaguptaka) nuns: stated without dates or numbers; confirm.
Views presented without ranking: Theravada objection on lineage grounds, supporters' view, Tibetan study, nuns content with current vows. Keeper should check fairness.
Index word is the title head 'The nuns return'; kept exactly.
